--- title: "Tool 1 — The Model-Free Ladder" subtitle: "Pearson · Spearman · Distance Correlation" --- *Learn-the-tool track · Lab 1 of 3.* This lab walks the **no-density road**: the measures that compare $X$ and $Y$ directly from samples, never needing a probability distribution. By the end you will have computed all three on the real basket, seen where they agree and where they split, and felt the `compare(transform(x), transform(y))` template through your own hands. **What you will produce:** a ranked table of every pair in the basket by each measure, and a clear answer to "when does the cheap tool suffice, and when does it lie?" --- ## Setup — load the real basket ::: {#480d575c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"])) tickers = list(R.columns) print(f"Loaded {len(R)} trading days × {len(tickers)} stocks") print(f" {R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()}") R.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loaded 1258 trading days × 14 stocks 2013-02-11 → 2018-02-07 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: --- ## 1 · The template, made literal Every measure on this road has the same shape: ``` Pearson = corr( x , y ) # transform = identity Spearman = corr( rank(x) , rank(y) ) # transform = rank distance corr = dcor( x , y ) # distance-matrix association ``` Let's run all three on the two running characters from the lecture. ::: {#f166beaa .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def trio_print(ticker_a, ticker_b): x, y = R[ticker_a].values, R[ticker_b].values t = measure_trio(x, y) la, lb = label.get(ticker_a, ticker_a), label.get(ticker_b, ticker_b) print(f"{la:>15s} & {lb:<15s} " f"Pearson={t['pearson']:+.3f} " f"Spearman={t['spearman']:+.3f} " f"distance={t['distance']:.3f}") return t print("Pair Pearson Spearman distance") print("-" * 68) _ = trio_print("JPM", "BAC") # two banks _ = trio_print("JPM", "KO") # bank vs. staple _ = trio_print("XOM", "CVX") # two energy majors ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pair Pearson Spearman distance -------------------------------------------------------------------- JPMorgan & Bank of Am. Pearson=+0.833 Spearman=+0.800 distance=0.785 JPMorgan & Coca-Cola Pearson=+0.291 Spearman=+0.279 distance=0.285 Exxon & Chevron Pearson=+0.774 Spearman=+0.748 distance=0.726 ``` ::: ::: For roughly elliptical daily equity returns the three measures land close together — which is exactly what we expect when the relationship is nearly linear. That agreement is *informative*: it says the no-density road already tells you most of the story. --- ## 2 · When do they disagree? Three measures agree on the bulk. They split on **tails** and **non-monotone** structure. Manufacture those two cases: ::: {#d4cc5e3b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 500 # U-shape: strong dependence, zero Pearson and Spearman x_u = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5, n) y_u = x_u**2 + 0.4 * rng.normal(size=n) # Tail-crash injection on a real pair x_real = R["JPM"].values.copy() y_real = R["BAC"].values.copy() crash_mask = (x_real < np.percentile(x_real, 5)) & (y_real < np.percentile(y_real, 5)) # Amplify the crash tail 2× x_amp, y_amp = x_real.copy(), y_real.copy() x_amp[crash_mask] *= 2.0 y_amp[crash_mask] *= 2.0 print("Case Pearson Spearman distance") print("-" * 55) for (name, x, y) in [ ("U-shape (synthetic)", x_u, y_u), ("JPM/BAC real", x_real, y_real), ("JPM/BAC tail-amplified", x_amp, y_amp), ]: t = measure_trio(x, y) print(f" {name:<24s} {t['pearson']:+.3f} {t['spearman']:+.3f} {t['distance']:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Case Pearson Spearman distance ------------------------------------------------------- U-shape (synthetic) -0.059 -0.048 0.477 JPM/BAC real +0.833 +0.800 0.785 JPM/BAC tail-amplified +0.886 +0.800 0.815 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-disagreement .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2)) axL.scatter(x_u, y_u, s=10, c=WARM, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none") tu = measure_trio(x_u, y_u) axL.set_title("U-shape (strong dep, Pearson≈0)", fontsize=11) annotate_box(axL, 0.5, -0.10, f"P={tu['pearson']:+.3f} S={tu['spearman']:+.3f} d={tu['distance']:.3f}") despine(axL) axR.scatter(x_real[~crash_mask], y_real[~crash_mask], s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="bulk") axR.scatter(x_real[crash_mask], y_real[crash_mask], s=18, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label="crash days") tr = measure_trio(x_real, y_real) axR.set_title("JPM / BAC — crash days highlighted", fontsize=11) annotate_box(axR, 0.5, -0.10, f"P={tr['pearson']:+.3f} S={tr['spearman']:+.3f} d={tr['distance']:.3f}") axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False) despine(axR) for ax in (axL, axR): ax.set_xlabel("X"); ax.set_ylabel("Y") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![U-shape and tail-amplified pair: where the measures split.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-disagreement-output-1.png){#fig-disagreement width=1304 height=489} ::: ::: --- ## 3 · Full basket ranking Compute all three measures for every pair; rank by distance correlation. ::: {#8d0b7c82 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import itertools rows = [] for a, b in itertools.combinations(tickers, 2): t = measure_trio(R[a].values, R[b].values) s_a, s_b = sector.get(a, "?"), sector.get(b, "?") rows.append(dict( pair=f"{a}/{b}", sector_match=(s_a == s_b), **t, )) rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["distance"], reverse=True) print(f"{'Pair':<12s} {'Pearson':>8s} {'Spearman':>9s} {'distance':>9s} same sector") print("-" * 60) for r in rows[:10]: print(f" {r['pair']:<10s} {r['pearson']:+8.3f} {r['spearman']:+9.3f} " f"{r['distance']:9.3f} {'✓' if r['sector_match'] else ''}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pair Pearson Spearman distance same sector ------------------------------------------------------------ BAC/C +0.851 +0.843 0.821 ✓ JPM/C +0.850 +0.832 0.813 ✓ JPM/BAC +0.833 +0.800 0.785 ✓ DUK/SO +0.800 +0.801 0.774 ✓ C/GS +0.799 +0.789 0.766 ✓ JPM/GS +0.809 +0.780 0.763 ✓ BAC/GS +0.777 +0.753 0.730 ✓ JPM/WFC +0.772 +0.746 0.726 ✓ XOM/CVX +0.774 +0.748 0.726 ✓ BAC/WFC +0.747 +0.735 0.712 ✓ ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## What to look for Within-sector pairs dominate the top. Cross-sector pairs where distance correlation *exceeds* Spearman by more than 0.05 are your candidates for non-linear or tail dependence — worth investigating with mutual information (Tool 2) or a tail-crash analysis (Job C). ::: --- ## 4 · Your turn — the cheapest tool that suffices For each pair below, decide: does Pearson already tell the story, or do you need to climb the ladder? | Pair | Pearson | Spearman | distance | Verdict | |------|---------|----------|----------|---------| | (fill in from your ranking) | | | | | **Rule of thumb:** if $|P - S| < 0.05$ and $|S - d| < 0.05$, the relationship is close to linear/elliptical and Pearson is fine. Any larger gap signals something the cheap tool is missing.
